etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English respect, from Old French respect, also respit (“respect, regard, consideration”), from Latin respectus (“a looking at, regard, respect”), perfect passive participle of respiciō (“look at, look back upon, respect”), from re- (“back”) + speciō (“to see”). Doublet of respite.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) an attitude of consideration or high regard

quote.citation: 2022 October 15, “Tajik President's Demand For 'Respect' From Putin Viewed Millions Of Times On YouTube”, in Radio Free Europe‎[1], archived from the original on 17 October 2022‎[2]:
quote.text: A video of Tajik President Emomali Rahmon complaining to Russian President Vladimir Putin about his lack of respect for the countries of Central Asia that were once part of the Soviet Union has struck a nerve on social media, where it has been viewed millions of times. […] “We have always respected the interests of our main strategic partner,” Rahmon said, referring to Russia. “We want respect, too."

definitions.definition: (uncountable, always plural) Polite greetings, often offered as condolences after a death.
(countable) a particular aspect, feature or detail of something

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 36”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: In our two loves there is but one respect

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 2:25:
quote.text: And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God had respect unto them.

definitions.definition: To have regard for something, to observe a custom, practice, rule or right.
To take notice of; to regard as worthy of special consideration; to heed.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), [William Shakespeare], The Tragedie of King Richard the Second. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  Valentine Simmes for Androw Wise, […], published 1597, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:

1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “New Atlantis. A Worke Vnfinished.”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC, page 33:
quote.text: We haue also large and various Orchards, and Gardens; Wherein we doe not ſo much reſpect Beauty, as Variety of Ground and Soile, proper for diuerſe Trees and Herbs: [...]

definitions.definition: (transitive, dated except in "respecting") To relate to; to be concerned with.

quote.text: Whatever they are else, they are always chastisements; and correction respects faults.

quote.citation: 1806, James Lee, An Introduction to Botany:
quote.text: Glandulation respects the secretory vessels, which are either glandules, follicles, or utricles.

quote.citation: 1859 December 13, Charles Dickens, “The Mortals in the House”, in Charles Dickens, editor, The Haunted House. The Extra Christmas Number of All the Year Round […], volume II, London:  […]  C[harles] Whiting, […], →OCLC, page 4, column 2:
quote.text: I hope I may never again be in a state of mind so unchristian as the mental frame in which I lived for some weeks, respecting the memory of Master B.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To regard; to consider; to deem.

quote.citation: c. 1597, Ben. Jonson, A Pleasant Comedy, Called: The Case is Alterd. […], London:  […]  [Nicholas Okes] for Bartholomew Sutton, and William Barrenger, […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: [T]his my friend (knowen by no name) was found, / Being then a child and ſcarce of power to ſpeake, / To whom my father gaue this name of Gaſper, / And as his own reſpected him to death, [...]That is, regarded him as his own.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, “Of East and West”, in Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC, 6th book, page 263:
quote.text: That Palladius adviſeth the front of his edifice ſhould ſo reſpect the South, that in the firſt angle it receive the riſing raies of the winter Sunne, and decline a little from the winter ſetting thereof.
